subject: Neurology
vignette: A patient sustains a hemisection of the right half of the spinal cord at T10. The clinician is asked to predict the sensory and motor findings that will appear below the level of the lesion.
question: Which of the following patterns of loss is expected below the lesion?

options.text: Ipsilateral loss of pain and temperature with contralateral loss of proprioception and vibration
Bilateral loss of all sensation below the lesion
Ipsilateral lower motor neuron signs below the lesion with contralateral upper motor neuron signs at the level
Ipsilateral loss of proprioception, vibration, and fine touch with contralateral loss of pain, temperature, and crude touch
Contralateral upper motor neuron signs below the lesion with an ipsilateral Horner syndrome

explanation_correct: In Brown-Sequard syndrome from cord hemisection, below the lesion the dorsal columns produce ipsilateral loss of proprioception, vibration, and fine two-point touch, while the spinothalamic tract produces contralateral loss of pain, temperature, and crude touch. At the lesion level there is ipsilateral loss of all sensation and ipsilateral lower motor neuron signs, and below the lesion there are ipsilateral upper motor neuron signs. This matches answer D.

explanation_incorrect.A: The modalities are reversed: pain and temperature are lost contralaterally and proprioception and vibration are lost ipsilaterally.
explanation_incorrect.B: Brown-Sequard produces a crossed pattern of deficits, not the bilateral loss of all sensation that follows complete cord transection.
explanation_incorrect.C: Lower motor neuron signs occur at the lesion level and upper motor neuron signs occur ipsilaterally below the lesion, so this pattern is incorrect.
explanation_incorrect.E: Upper motor neuron signs are ipsilateral below the lesion, and Horner syndrome occurs only with lesions above T1, not at T10.

educationalObjective: Brown-Sequard below the lesion causes ipsilateral proprioception, vibration, and fine touch loss with contralateral pain, temperature, and crude touch loss.

subject: Neurology
vignette: A patient has a hemisection of the left half of the spinal cord at C8, just above T1. In addition to the classic sensory and motor findings, the clinician notes an ipsilateral ptosis and miosis.
question: Which of the following best explains this additional finding?

options.text: Involvement of the oculosympathetic pathway in a lesion above T1, causing ipsilateral Horner syndrome
Involvement of the spinothalamic tract causing contralateral facial sensory loss
Involvement of the dorsal columns causing ipsilateral facial proprioception loss
Involvement of the corticospinal tract causing contralateral hemiparesis
Involvement of the anterior horn causing ipsilateral flaccid paralysis at the level

explanation_correct: In Brown-Sequard syndrome, when the hemisection occurs above T1, involvement of the oculosympathetic pathway produces an ipsilateral Horner syndrome with ptosis, miosis, and anhidrosis. This is a classic associated finding of a high cord hemisection and explains the eye findings in this patient.

explanation_incorrect.B: The spinothalamic tract carries contralateral body pain and temperature sensation below the lesion; it does not cause Horner syndrome or facial sensory loss from a cord hemisection.
explanation_incorrect.C: The dorsal columns carry ipsilateral body proprioception and vibration below the lesion and do not produce Horner syndrome.
explanation_incorrect.D: Corticospinal tract involvement causes ipsilateral upper motor neuron signs below the lesion, not contralateral hemiparesis, and does not explain ptosis and miosis.
explanation_incorrect.E: Anterior horn involvement causes ipsilateral lower motor neuron signs at the lesion level, not the oculosympathetic findings of Horner syndrome.

educationalObjective: A Brown-Sequard lesion above T1 can disrupt the oculosympathetic pathway, causing ipsilateral Horner syndrome.

subject: Neurology
vignette: A child presents with a staggering gait, frequent falling, nystagmus, and dysarthria. Examination shows pes cavus, hammer toes, loss of deep tendon reflexes, and kyphoscoliosis. He also has hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Cerebral palsy
Friedreich ataxia
Subacute combined degeneration
Spinal muscular atrophy
Poliomyelitis

explanation_correct: Friedreich ataxia is an autosomal recessive trinucleotide repeat disorder with a GAA expansion on chromosome 9 in the frataxin gene, causing mitochondrial impairment. It causes degeneration of the lateral corticospinal tract with spastic paralysis, the spinocerebellar tract with ataxia, the dorsal columns with reduced vibration and proprioception, and dorsal root ganglia with loss of deep tendon reflexes. Findings include staggering gait, nystagmus, dysarthria, pes cavus, hammer toes, diabetes mellitus, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy as the cause of death, and childhood kyphoscoliosis.

explanation_incorrect.A: Cerebral palsy is a nonprogressive motor disorder from perinatal injury with spasticity and persistent primitive reflexes, not a progressive GAA repeat disorder with cardiomyopathy and pes cavus.
explanation_incorrect.C: Subacute combined degeneration is vitamin B12 deficiency with dorsal column, corticospinal, and spinocerebellar demyelination and upper motor neuron signs with increased reflexes, not the frataxin disorder with absent reflexes and cardiomyopathy.
explanation_incorrect.D: Spinal muscular atrophy is an SMN1 mutation causing pure lower motor neuron floppy baby with tongue fasciculations, not multisystem ataxia with pes cavus and cardiomyopathy.
explanation_incorrect.E: Poliomyelitis is an acute viral anterior horn disease with asymmetric lower motor neuron weakness, not a chronic progressive ataxia with cardiomyopathy.

educationalObjective: Friedreich ataxia is an AR GAA/frataxin disorder causing spinocerebellar, corticospinal, dorsal column, and DRG degeneration with ataxia, pes cavus, and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

subject: Neurology
vignette: A 12-year-old girl with progressive ataxia and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy undergoes genetic testing. Analysis shows an expanded GAA trinucleotide repeat on chromosome 9 in a gene encoding an iron-binding protein involved in mitochondrial function.
question: Which of the following best describes the inheritance pattern and the affected gene product?

options.text: Autosomal dominant repeat in huntingtin affecting the basal ganglia
X-linked recessive mutation in dystrophin affecting skeletal muscle
Autosomal recessive SMN1 mutation affecting snRNP assembly
Mitochondrial DNA mutation affecting oxidative phosphorylation
Autosomal recessive GAA repeat in frataxin affecting mitochondrial iron handling

explanation_correct: Friedreich ataxia is an autosomal recessive trinucleotide repeat disorder with a GAA expansion on chromosome 9 in the gene encoding frataxin, an iron-binding protein. The repeat impairs mitochondrial function and produces degeneration of corticospinal, spinocerebellar, dorsal column, and dorsal root ganglion pathways, with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy as the cause of death. This case matches both the autosomal recessive inheritance and the frataxin gene product.

explanation_incorrect.A: An autosomal dominant huntingtin repeat causes Huntington disease with chorea and basal ganglia pathology, not frataxin or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
explanation_incorrect.B: X-linked dystrophin mutations cause Duchenne or Becker muscular dystrophy, not a GAA repeat in frataxin with this ataxia phenotype.
explanation_incorrect.C: An autosomal recessive SMN1 mutation causes spinal muscular atrophy with lower motor neuron degeneration and a floppy baby, not a GAA repeat in frataxin.
explanation_incorrect.D: A mitochondrial DNA mutation would show maternal inheritance, not an autosomal recessive nuclear GAA repeat in frataxin.

educationalObjective: Friedreich ataxia is an AR GAA repeat expansion in the frataxin gene on chromosome 9, disrupting mitochondrial iron handling.

subject: Neurology
vignette: A 3-year-old with a history of prematurity and low birth weight has persistent spasticity in both legs, hyperreflexia, abnormal posture, and persistence of primitive reflexes. His motor skill development is delayed. Imaging shows periventricular leukomalacia.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Friedreich ataxia
Spinal muscular atrophy
Cerebral palsy
Poliomyelitis
Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis

explanation_correct: Cerebral palsy is permanent motor dysfunction resulting from nonprogressive injury to the developing fetal or infant brain and is the most common movement disorder in children. Prematurity and low birth weight are the strongest risk factors, with associated periventricular leukomalacia. It presents with upper motor neuron signs such as spasticity and hyperreflexia in one or more limbs, persistent primitive reflexes, abnormal posture, and delayed motor development. This case is classic.

explanation_incorrect.A: Friedreich ataxia is a progressive autosomal recessive GAA and frataxin disorder with ataxia, pes cavus, and cardiomyopathy, not a nonprogressive injury with prematurity and periventricular leukomalacia.
explanation_incorrect.B: Spinal muscular atrophy is an SMN1 mutation causing lower motor neuron floppy baby with tongue fasciculations, not upper motor neuron spasticity with persistent primitive reflexes.
explanation_incorrect.D: Poliomyelitis is an acute viral anterior horn disease with asymmetric lower motor neuron weakness, not a chronic nonprogressive upper motor neuron disorder.
explanation_incorrect.E: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis is a progressive combined upper and lower motor neuron degeneration of adults, not a nonprogressive childhood injury associated with prematurity.

educationalObjective: Cerebral palsy is a nonprogressive perinatal brain injury (prematurity, PVL) causing UMN spasticity, hyperreflexia, and persistent primitive reflexes.

subject: Neurology
vignette: A pregnant woman at high risk for preterm delivery is given magnesium sulfate prenatally to reduce the incidence and severity of a chronic childhood motor disorder. The disorder is nonprogressive, associated with periventricular leukomalacia, and treated with baclofen, botulinum toxin injections, or selective dorsal rhizotomy.
question: Which of the following disorders is this intervention intended to prevent?

options.text: Friedreich ataxia
Subacute combined degeneration
Poliomyelitis
Cerebral palsy
Spinal muscular atrophy

explanation_correct: Cerebral palsy results from nonprogressive fetal or infant brain injury, with prematurity and low birth weight as the strongest risk factors and periventricular leukomalacia as an associated finding. Prenatal magnesium sulfate given in high-risk pregnancies reduces the incidence and severity of cerebral palsy. Treatment includes muscle relaxants such as baclofen, botulinum toxin injections, and selective dorsal rhizotomy, matching the vignette.

explanation_incorrect.A: Friedreich ataxia is a genetic GAA and frataxin disorder; magnesium sulfate does not prevent it and baclofen or rhizotomy are not its treatments.
explanation_incorrect.B: Subacute combined degeneration is due to vitamin B12 deficiency and is prevented by adequate vitamin B12, not by magnesium sulfate.
explanation_incorrect.C: Poliomyelitis is a viral infection prevented by vaccination, not by prenatal magnesium sulfate.
explanation_incorrect.E: Spinal muscular atrophy is a genetic SMN1 disorder; it is not prevented by magnesium sulfate and is not treated with baclofen or rhizotomy.

educationalObjective: Prenatal magnesium sulfate reduces the incidence and severity of cerebral palsy in high-risk pregnancies; CP is a nonprogressive injury causing UMN spasticity.
